<explanation>
Below is a step‐by‐step instruction on how to create an accurate and detailed system design diagram for this project – the 微信 Markdown 编辑器 (WeChat Markdown Editor). This project is primarily a single-page web application built with Vue3 (using Vite) for live Markdown rendering and editing, but it also provides a CLI tool (md-cli) and Docker-based deployment options. There is even a Go-based server (located in docker/latest/server/main.go) used in some deployment scenarios, which means we have a mix of frontend, backend/service layers, and deployment/build configuration. Here’s how you can break it down:

1. Identify the Main Components
   • Frontend Application:
     - The core UI lives in the /src directory (with Vue components, entry points, utilities, etc.). This part includes the markdown editor, preview panes, UI components (in subdirectories such as /components and /components/ui), and configuration files (found under /src/config and /src/lib).
     - Entry points (like the popup in /src/entrypoints and the background script) support different modes of operation.
   • CLI & Local Deployment:
     - The md-cli directory contains a Node.js–based command-line interface that users can install globally. This tool allows you to quickly spin up a private version of the editor.
   • Docker & Server Components:
     - The docker folder includes several Dockerfiles (Dockerfile.base, Dockerfile.nginx, Dockerfile.standalone, Dockerfile.static) and scripts to build images, push images, and release.
     - The docker/latest/server/main.go is a Go-based server which may be responsible for handling API requests (for example, file uploads or serving built assets) when deployed in certain environments.
   • CI/CD & Configuration:
     - The .github/workflows directory (with multiple workflow YAML files) shows the automated build, release, and deployment pipeline for this project.
     - Additional configuration files (editorconfig, .nvmrc, .vscode, eslint.config.mjs, postcss.config.js, etc.) help manage coding standards, build scripts, and deployment options.
   • External Integrations:
     - The README details support for multiple external image-hosting services (GitHub, Aliyun OSS, Tencent Cloud, etc.) along with a customizable upload logic.
     - The system thus interacts with these external services for file uploads, which should be represented as external components.

2. Define the Relationships and Data Flow
   • User Interaction:
     - The user accesses the application via a web browser (Chrome is recommended) that loads index.html along with the bundled Vue application.
     - The application (editor UI) processes Markdown in real time (using utilities in /src/utils and rendering functions) and sends image uploads via API calls.
   • Frontend ⇄ Backend Interaction:
     - The Vue application might interact with a backend service (provided either by the md-cli Node.js server or the Go-based server run via Docker) via RESTful APIs for operations like file upload and content management.
   • CLI / Docker Deployment:
     - The md-cli tool acts as an alternative way to launch the service in a local environment.
     - The Docker images (referenced in the docker/ folder) package the application for containerized environments. The diagram should show how these containers are built (using the scripts in /scripts) and deployed.
   • CI/CD Pipeline:
     - Represent the GitHub Actions workflows (build, release, docker builds) that automatically trigger builds and deploys, ensuring a smooth integration/delivery pipeline.
   • External Services:
     - Add components for external image-hosting services, indicating that the editor may send file uploads to third-party APIs based on configured tokens and parameters.

3. Architectural Patterns and Key Technologies
   • Architectural Separation:
     - The diagram should clearly split the project into the frontend (Vue3 & Vite), backend/API layer (Node.js via md-cli and/or Go-based server in Docker), and deployment pipelines.
   • Technologies & Frameworks:
     - Frontend: Vue3, Vite, Tailwind (as inferred from tailwind.config.cjs), and various UI libraries/components.
     - Backend: Node.js (for md-cli) and Go (in the Docker/server image).
     - Build & Deployment: Docker, GitHub Actions, and associated shell scripts (in the /scripts directory).
   • Design Principles:
     - Emphasize modular design (as shown by well-organized directories for components, utilities, stores, and types) and separation of concerns (frontend UI vs backend operations vs deployment configurations).

4. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram
   • For a full-stack application like this:
     - Clearly distinguish between the browser-based editor (frontend SPA) and the backend/service layers.
     - Show how the CLI tool (md-cli) serves as an alternative mode for deploying and testing the app.
     - Represent the Dockerized environments and how they encapsulate the Go server plus any reverse proxy (nginx) or static file serving.
   • Label each part appropriately:
     - Use clear labels such as “Vue3 Frontend”, “Markdown Rendering Engine”, “md-cli (Node.js Server)”, “Go API Server”, “Docker Build Environment”, “CI/CD Pipeline”, and “External Image Hosting Services”.
   • Draw directional arrows:
     - Indicate data flow from the User’s browser to the front-end application.
     - Show API calls from the front-end to the backend.
     - Display upload flow from the UI through the backend to external services.
     - Illustrate deployment flows (from GitHub Actions through Docker builds to production).
   • Use color coding and shapes:
     - For instance, rectangles for app components, cylinders (or database symbols) for storage/external services, and clouds to denote external services.
     - Different colors can represent different layers: one color for frontend components, another for backend services, and yet another for deployment/infrastructure.

5. Essential Elements to Include in the Diagram
   • Clear components for each major part:
     - “User Browser” (client)
     - “Vue3 Editor Application” (frontend that includes real-time markdown processing, custom themes, and rich UI components)
     - “md-cli Node.js Server” (local deployment and serving of the editor)
     - “Go-based API Server” (part of the Docker deployment for handling API requests)
     - “Docker & Build Scripts” (containerized environments with multiple Dockerfiles and build scripts)
     - “CI/CD Pipeline” (GitHub Actions build/release workflows)
     - “External Image Hosting Services” (multiple third-party integrations for file uploads)
   • Directional arrows to indicate:
     - The flow of user interactions (input, preview, file upload).
     - Data flow from the frontend to the backend.
     - Automated deployment flows via CI/CD actions.
   • Annotations or legends:
     - Define color schemes, shapes, and line styles used to represent each type of component.

6. Final Considerations
   • Be very detailed – capture each deployment and build configuration as its own component if needed (don’t hesitate to over-segment based on the codebase’s structure).
   • Do not overcomplicate the diagram but ensure each essential piece (frontend, backend/service, docker deployment, external integrations, and CI/CD pipelines) is represented.
   • Keep the diagram flexible; you may use separate sub-diagrams if needed (for example, one for the deployment pipeline and another for application data flow) while ensuring the overall architecture remains clear.

By following these instructions, you will create a comprehensive system design diagram that accurately represents the 微信 Markdown 编辑器’s architecture and deployment strategies. This detailed separation of components, combined with clear labeling, directional flows, and color coding, will provide a quick and complete understanding of how all parts work together within the project.
</explanation>
